query: For noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials used in catalysis, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs reliable material formation and the resulting catalytic performance, and why? Specify one controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: When using noble metal single‐source precursors, the coordination strength of the precursor ligands (e.g., acetylacetonate vs. citrate) governs the reduction kinetics and local atomic mobility, such that stronger ligand binding restricts atomic mobility during dropwise reduction. This enhanced restriction promotes more uniform, single-phase HEA formation with fewer structural defects, which in turn leads to improved catalytic performance (e.g., higher turnover frequency in ORR or HER).
generation.material_initial_state: A mixed-metal precursor solution containing noble metal ions (e.g., Pt, Pd, Ir, Ru, Rh) coordinated by standard ligands (e.g., acetylacetonate) or modified with stronger coordinating ligands (e.g., citrate) in an appropriate polyol solvent.
generation.intervention: Replace standard acetylacetonate ligands with a stronger coordinating ligand (e.g., citrate) in otherwise identical single‐source precursor formulations, and conduct dropwise reduction synthesis under fixed low-temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature polyol synthesis with controlled dropwise injection rate, identical solvent, temperature, and reduction gas mixture. The only variable is the precursor ligand environment (strong vs. weak coordination).
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of atomic mixing/uniformity and defect density in the resulting HEA nanoparticles, as characterized by in situ (or ex situ) XAS, high-resolution TEM, and phase analysis (XRD).
generation.mechanism: Stronger coordinating ligands raise the kinetic barrier for precursor reduction, thereby further restricting atomic mobility during nucleation and growth. This results in more stochastic yet homogeneous incorporation of each metal atom, reducing the formation of segregated regions or defects. In turn, the electronic structure of the well-mixed HEA (e.g., optimal charge transfer and uniform d-band characteristics) enhances the catalytic active sites for target reactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (HEA nanoparticles synthesized with acetylacetonate ligands), the HEAs prepared with stronger coordinating ligands (citrate-based precursors) will exhibit higher phase uniformity and reduced defect density, which will correlate with an enhanced catalytic performance (e.g., 30–50% increase in current density or turnover frequency in ORR or HER tests).
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized under identical dropwise low-temperature conditions using acetylacetonate-ligated noble metal precursors.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in solution-based, low-temperature reduction syntheses of noble metal HEA nanoparticles (typically composed of the platinum group metals) where precursor mobility is limiting; it may not extend to high-temperature methods (e.g., Joule heating) in which rapid diffusion dominates.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between ligand coordination strength and atomic mixing is not yet established. This study extends findings from PMC10621632 (which emphasizes precursor mobility control in dropwise synthesis) and PMC10171813 (which shows that controlling dropwise injection affects nanostructure) by isolating precursor coordination as an independent variable. The exact improvement magnitude in catalytic performance remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of noble metal HEA nanoparticles under identical dropwise, low-temperature polyol reduction conditions. In one batch, use standard acetylacetonate-ligated precursors. In the other, use analogous precursors complexed with a stronger coordinating ligand (e.g., citrate). Characterize the resulting nanoparticles for phase purity, defect density, and degree of atomic mixing via HR-TEM, XAS, and XRD. Then, assess the catalytic performance (e.g., through ORR or HER electrochemical testing) under identical testing conditions.
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy for defect and morphology analysis
X-ray absorption spectroscopy for local electronic structure and atomic mixing verification
Electrochemical measurements (current density, overpotential, turnover frequency) for catalytic activity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant differences in atomic mixing, defect density, or catalytic performance (within experimental error) are observed between the two batches—despite the change in precursor ligand—then the hypothesis that precursor coordination (ligand effects) governs the reliable formation of single-phase, high-performance HEAs is falsified.

Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. In a typical experiment, the multi-elemental salt precursor mixture (0.05 M in ethanol) was first deposited on an activated carbon nanofiber matrix (see Methods in the Supplementary Materials) with uniform wetting (Fig. 2B). After applying the rapid high-temperature heating (500 ms, 1500 K) to the substrate, the precursor salt mixture was thermally reduced into metals and well mixed at high temperature; upon quenching, the uniform mixing self-assembled into small NPs dispersed on the substrate (Fig. 2C). Figure 2D displays the temporal evolution of the temperature during the synthesis, showing featured rapid heating and cooling that enable the alloy NP formation. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple elements in near-equiatomic proportions hold great promise in heterogeneous catalysis because of their exceptional physicochemical properties governed by synergy. Herein, we prepared PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles via a one-step colloid-based route and tested their catalytic performance for nitrobenzene hydrogenation to aniline. The SiO2 supported PtPdCoCuNi displays 93.9% yield of aniline at 80 °C, which is 2.11 times that of PtPd/SiO2. Even at room temperature, a 47.4% yield of aniline is attained with the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst. DRIFTS experiments indicate formation of isolated Pt and Pd sites after alloying the transition metals and evidence a stronger interaction between the HEA catalyst and nitrobenzene. Both XPS data and DFT calculations disclose charge transfer to Pt and Pd species, which eventually enhance the interaction between nitrobenzene and the isolated metal sites and the hydrogenation activity as well. The experimental and theoretical results shed light on mechanistic understanding of the unique catalytic performance of the HEA nanocatalyst and pave a new avenue to realize the high catalytic performance of nitrobenze
